reels.title: A dinner plate from 1616

prediction.prompt: In 1616 Dirk Hartog nailed a pewter plate to a post on an island off western Australia. When did the next European find it?

frames.text: On 25 October 1616, Dirk Hartog reached an island off western Australia. This is the pewter plate he left there.
frames.say: On the twenty-fifth of October, sixteen sixteen, Dirk Hartog reached an island off western Australia. This is the pewter plate he left there.

frames.text: He landed at Cape Inscription, the island's northern tip, and nailed the plate to a post on the cliff top.
In 1697 another Dutch captain, Willem de Vlamingh, came ashore and found it.
frames.say: In sixteen ninety-seven another Dutch captain, Willem de Vlahming, came ashore and found it.

frames.text: He put up a new plate, and the original went back to the Netherlands. It is now in the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam.
It is the oldest known surviving object from European exploration of Australia. The island, Wirruwana to the Malgana people, now bears Hartog's name.
frames.say: It is the oldest known surviving object from European exploration of Australia. The island, Wirroo-wahna to the Malgana people, now bears Hartog's name.

reels.takeaway: Hartog's plate marked his landing in 1616. Willem de Vlamingh removed it in 1697, and it is now in the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam.
